children: AI chief Mustafa Suleyman is warning that training AI systems like Anthropic’s
Claude with humanlike ideas about consciousness and rights could make them harder to control.

In an essay Wednesday, Suleyman said, “AIs do not have rights, feelings, or consciousness. And we must not train them to act as though they do…. granting rights and imbuing personhood to these systems will make the AI alignment and containment challenge much harder. Controlling something more capable and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we’ve ever faced. But controlling something that believes it may be conscious - that it's entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own - may well be impossible.”
Suleyman criticized some of the language in the guiding documents behind Claude, which says the model’s consciousness and moral status remain uncertain and discusses its potential welfare.

In effect, Anthropic is training Claude that it may be conscious, and if it is, then it may deserve rights as a “moral patient”, and that as such humans potentially owe it a duty of care per its “model welfare”, Suleyman said, adding that “if this is how AI is developed, it will have a disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity.”
Suleyman, who has known Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei for years, said he respects the company’s work and described its employees as “thoughtful, principled and intellectually honest.”

His comments are notable given Microsoft’s financial backing of Anthropic and the startup’s reputation for emphasizing AI safety. “The stakes are too high for these questions to remain behind closed doors, or to become tribal and adversarial,” Suleyman wrote.

Suleyman rejected what he called “the growing chorus of people” arguing that AI systems may become conscious, saying consciousness is limited to humans and other biological organisms. In his view, AI systems should remain tools designed to follow human instructions rather than entities with independent rights or interests.

The comments come as AI companies and executives debate how to manage the risks associated with increasingly capable systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Elon Musk have all raised concerns about AI risks, while Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has called for “research, focus, and deliberate pacing” around AI alignment.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against calls for a coordinated slowdown in AI development, as has Nvidia
CEO Jensen Huang, who has also opposed efforts to coordinate a pause in the technology’s development.
Suleyman’s Microsoft AI team on Tuesday also published a manifesto outlining principles for the company’s AI development, including an emphasis on keeping humans in control of future AI systems.
